aboutAuthor: William Green has interviewed investing legends for over two decades for Time, Fortune, and Forbes. He distills those conversations into a humane guide that treats investing as a training ground for resilience, curiosity, and generosity.

points.heading: Clone the best teachers
points.body: Pabrai's motel-to-Buffett cloning shows humility is the shortcut: copy fee structure, filings, and focus, and replicate giving via Dakshana. A one-page checklist and index card keep the clone disciplined.

points.heading: Loneliness is a skill
points.body: Templeton in the Bahamas and the No one knows memo show that maximal discomfort often marks maximal opportunity. Design isolation via few trusted peers and rituals so consensus feels optional.

points.heading: Everything changes, so size accordingly
points.body: Miller's streak and collapse illustrate that permanence should not be capitalized and impermanence should not be despaired. Cost permanence versus performance transience, and journaled predictions, warn against extrapolation.

points.heading: Resilience is prebuilt
points.body: Survival after a sixty percent drawdown came from refusing leverage, keeping cash as sleep insurance, and pre-writing the next thesis from scratch. Four pillars diagram guides preparation before crisis.

points.heading: Simplicity compounds
points.body: Shubin Stein's one-page price-quality-people check and Mecham's Spartan Utah desk show that deleting inputs improves signal. The index card thesis forces clarity that complex models obscure.

points.heading: Share scale with customers
points.body: Nick and Zak's flywheel where Costco, Amazon, and Geico return scale as lower prices created the Nomad adventure. Closing at peak because size versus return slopes down proved discipline beats asset gathering.

insights: The motel Dhando framework heading risk, few bets, explains Pabrai's investing more than any Wall Street manual.
Nick and Zak's scale-shared flywheel that returned size to customers as price, compounding goodwill and economics.
Don't be a fool checklist: Enron footnote sprawl and Madoff smooth returns as red flags to pass, not puzzles to solve.
conclusion: Richer, Wiser, Happier finds that the habits that build great portfolios, cloning, solitude, simplicity, shared scale, and fool-avoidance, build better lives when applied to learning, relationships, and giving. Copy the habits, not the holdings, and let richer serve wiser and happier.
